source: Written for Wayword as a learner's guide; not part of the original dataset. Examples are dataset phrases.
intro: French spelling has many silent letters, but it is consistent. Get the nasal vowels, the u, and the r right and you'll sound much better right away.
reading: CAPITALS mark where the phrase lands. French stress is light and falls at the end of a word group.
"ahn", "ohn" and "an" at the end of a syllable are nasal vowels. Don't say the n.

sounds.name: Nasal vowels
sounds.how: Push the vowel through your nose and stop before the n. Non is a single nasal "oh", not "nonn".

sounds.name: U vs OU
sounds.how: For u, say "ee" and then round your lips tightly without moving your tongue. ou is a plain "oo". Tu (you) and tout (all) are different words.

sounds.name: French R
sounds.how: Made at the back of the throat with a light scrape, like a gentle gargle. The tip of your tongue stays down behind your bottom teeth.

sounds.name: Silent endings
sounds.how: Final consonants and the final e are usually silent: pas is "pah", toilettes is "twah-LET". The -ent ending on verbs is silent too.

sounds.name: Liaison
sounds.how: A normally silent final consonant is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel, and joins onto it: États-Unis is "zay-tah-zew-NEE".

sounds.name: Soft J and G
sounds.how: j, and g before e or i, = zh as in "measure".

sounds.name: The E family
sounds.how: é is a tight "ay" with no glide at the end. è, ê and ai are an open "eh".

tips_source: "How it's said" tips are written for Wayword (not part of the dataset): how a speaker of standard (Parisian) French says the phrase at normal speed, next to the careful pronunciation line.

tips.please: In everyday speech the l often drops out: see-voo-PLEH.
tips.dont_speak_well: At normal speed one of the two "uh" sounds drops: zhuhn parl pah byen frahn-SAY. In casual speech ne often disappears altogether: zhuh parl pah byen frahn-SAY.
tips.dont_understand: Ne shrinks to just n: zhuhn kohn-PRAHN pah. In casual speech it's often dropped altogether: zhuh kohn-PRAHN pah.
tips.speak_slowly: The middle e of lentement is silent at normal speed: lahnt-MAHN.
tips.what_mean: Qu'est-ce que is said as one quick word, kesk: kesk sah vuh DEER.
tips.learning_by_trying: En and essayant are always linked, the n carrying over: ahn-neh-say-YAHN. De loses its vowel: zhah-PRAHN ahn-neh-say-YAHN d'par-LAY.
tips.can_i_have: Je often loses its vowel and runs into peux, so it sounds like sh: shpuh ah-VWAHR.
tips.i_would_like: Je loses its vowel and runs into voudrais: zhvoo-DRAY.
tips.whats_in_this: Il y a is usually squeezed to "ee-yah", with no l: kes-kee-YAH duh-DAHN.
tips.dairy: Il y a is usually squeezed to "ee-yah", with no l: es-kee-YAH day proh-DWEE lay-TYAY.
tips.recommend_food: Qu'est-ce que shrinks to kesk, and the e of recommandez almost vanishes: kesk voo rkoh-mahn-DAY.
tips.tip_included: Service runs straight into est, its s starting the next syllable: luh sehr-VEE-seh kohn-PREE.
tips.people_tip: A sounded final consonant joins the next vowel: laisse un is "leh-SUHN", and pourboire ici is "poor-BWAH-ree-SEE".
tips.live_here: Habites runs into ici, its t starting the next syllable: tew ah-BEE-tee-SEE.
tips.been_america: In speech, tu es is usually squeezed to t'es, "tay": tay day-ZHAH ah-LAY oh zay-tah-zew-NEE.
tips.im_visiting: Suis usually links onto en with a z sound: zhuh swee-ZAHN vee-ZEET. In casual speech, je suis is often just "shwee".
tips.love_languages: The r of j'adore joins apprendre, and the -re at the end of apprendre is often clipped: zhah-DOH-rah-PRAHND lay LAHNG.
tips.youre_funny: In speech, tu es is usually squeezed to t'es: tay DROL.
tips.thanks_help: Ton links onto aide, its n starting the next syllable: mehr-SEE poor tohn-NED.
